title: How to Make Slowed and Reverb Songs – Free Guide
description: Learn how to make slowed and reverb music free in your browser: load a track, apply speed, reverb and bass, then export a WAV or MP3. No signup, no watermark.
h1: How to Make Slowed and Reverb
heroText: Slowed and reverb means lowering a song's speed and pitch while adding a reverb effect, so it plays back slower, deeper and dreamier than the original. You can do it free in your browser with [Slowed and Reverb Maker](/): load an MP3 or WAV, pick the Classic Slowed + Reverb preset, trim the section you want on the waveform, and export the result as WAV or MP3. No signup, no software install, and your audio never leaves your device.

sections.title: The Short Answer
sections.body:
To make a slowed and reverb edit, load the song into [Slowed and Reverb Maker](/), press the Classic Slowed + Reverb preset, listen, trim the part you want, and render. The preset is four numbers you can see on the console: speed 0.80×, pitch −2 semitones, reverb 55% and bass +4 dB. That combination is the deep, atmospheric version of a song people mean when they say slowed and reverb.

The two controls work together rather than independently: the speed slider slows the playback tape-style, so it drops the pitch along with the tempo — 0.80× alone is roughly four semitones down — and the pitch field then adds whole semitones on top. The preset sets both: 0.80× stretches the song out, and its −2 semitone field deepens that drop without making the vocal muddy. Start from the preset, listen to one verse, then move only the slider that feels wrong — speed first if the track drags or rushes, reverb second if the room is too small or too washy. Everything decodes, previews and renders inside your browser tab, with no upload and no account, and you can try it on the built-in sample before you pick a file.

sections.title: Step by Step
sections.body: The edit takes a couple of minutes once the file is on your device. Every step runs locally — the audio never leaves the tab.

steps.title: Save the song as an audio file
steps.body: Find the MP3, WAV, M4A, OGG, FLAC or AAC file you want to edit. The tool loads these straight from your device and draws the track as a playable waveform, so you can hear the original before you change anything.

steps.title: Load it into the browser tool
steps.body: Open Slowed and Reverb Maker and press Choose file, or drop the file on the loader. The waveform appears with the track name, format and length. If you just want to hear the effect first, press Try the sample for a short pad you can edit without finding a file.

steps.title: Pick the Classic Slowed + Reverb preset
steps.body: The preset sets speed to 0.80×, pitch to −2 semitones, reverb to 55% and bass boost to +4 dB. That is the sound most people mean by slowed and reverb. If your song is already dark and dense, drop the reverb a little before you touch anything else.

steps.title: Fine-tune speed and pitch
steps.body: Listen to the first verse at 0.80×. If it drags, try 0.85×; for the deeper classic feel go to 0.75×. Pitch adds whole semitones from −12 to +12 on top of the drop the speed setting already makes, so a field of −1 to −2 keeps voices believable while −4 and below heads toward daycore.

steps.title: Trim to the section you want
steps.body: Drag the trim handles on the waveform, or type the start and end in seconds, to cut the track down to the 30–60 second hook you plan to post. Ending on the last word of a phrase sounds better than a cut mid-vowel.

steps.title: Preview, then render WAV or MP3
steps.body: Play the trimmed section once more with the reverb on — the tail runs about 1.6 seconds past the end, so leave a little room. Then press Render: the tool renders the edit offline in your browser and offers a WAV file or a 192 kbps MP3, matching what you just heard.

sections.title: The Settings Explained
sections.body: Four numbers shape the slowed and reverb sound. You do not need to understand signal processing to use them, but knowing what each one does helps you fix a mix that feels off instead of guessing.

items.title: Speed
items.body: Speed multiplies playback tempo, from 0.5× to 1.5× in fine steps. At 0.80× a three-minute song runs about 3:45. Below 0.7× most vocals smear and the beat loses its swing, so 0.75–0.85× is where the style lives. On this tool speed also lowers pitch as it slows, about four semitones at 0.80×, so the pitch field is there to correct or deepen that drop.

items.title: Pitch
items.body: Pitch shifts note height from −12 to +12 semitones. Slowing always drags pitch down with it, so the Classic preset's −2 semitones are added on top of the roughly four-semitone drop that 0.80× makes on its own. Push further for daycore; a positive value over a slow tempo gives the odd, bright slowed sound some edits use.

items.title: Reverb
items.body: Reverb adds the soft tail of a large room after each note. The 55% mix in the Classic preset is clearly audible space that still leaves the vocal in front. Sparse material such as piano or acoustic guitar takes 65–70%; dense mixes usually want less. At 0% the tail shrinks to a few milliseconds and the export stays dry.

items.title: Bass boost
items.body: Bass boost lifts the low end by 0 to 12 dB so a slower track keeps weight on phone speakers. The Classic preset uses +4 dB, which suits most songs; hip-hop and EDM already carry heavy lows and often need none. Raise it until the kick feels solid, not until the mix turns muddy.

faq.question: What speed is a slowed and reverb song?
faq.answer: Most slowed and reverb edits sit between 0.75× and 0.85× of the original speed, with 0.80× the common default. At 0.80× a three-minute song lasts roughly 3 minutes 45 seconds. Slowing playback drops pitch with it, about four semitones at 0.80×, and the Classic preset adds its −2 semitones on top, which is what gives the voice its deeper tone.

faq.question: How much reverb should I add?
faq.answer: Start at the 55% the Classic Slowed + Reverb preset uses: a clear room sound without burying the vocal. Sparse songs such as acoustic or piano tracks can take 65–70% for a dreamier feel, and dense mixes usually need less. The render adds a tail of about 1.6 seconds at any setting above zero.

faq.question: Can I make slowed and reverb on my phone?
faq.answer: Yes. The tool is a browser page, so it works in a mobile browser with nothing to install: load the file from your storage, apply the preset, trim on the waveform and render an MP3. The audio is decoded and rendered on your device, so the edit itself needs no network once the page has loaded.

faq.question: Does slowing a song change the pitch?
faq.answer: Yes. The speed slider slows the playback itself, so pitch falls with it: 0.80× drops every note about four semitones before the pitch field is touched. The Classic preset then adds −2 semitones on top, so the result sounds deep rather than merely slow. Move the pitch field the other way if you want a slow edit back near its original key.

faq.question: What format should I export?
faq.answer: Render WAV when the file goes into a video editor or another audio app — it is 16-bit lossless at your browser's audio rate, 44.1 kHz on most devices. Render MP3 when the clip is going straight to social media: it is 192 kbps and far smaller, so it uploads faster. Both are rendered offline from the same buffer you previewed, so neither surprises you.

faq.question: How is slowed and reverb different from nightcore?
faq.answer: They are opposite directions on the same dial. The Nightcore preset runs at 1.25× with +4 semitones and only 12% reverb for a bright, urgent sound; the slowed preset runs at 0.80× with −2 semitones and 55% reverb for a deep, relaxed one. The [full comparison](/slowed-vs-nightcore/) breaks down when to use each.
